# Errors {#sec-errors}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

R has one mechanism for failure: `stop()` signals an error, and the error travels up through every caller until a `tryCatch()` handles it or R reports it at the top level. Rust has two. A *panic*, which @sec-types and @sec-drop showed, is for bugs: states the program wasn't written to handle. Failures that a program should expect, such as text that isn't a number, are ordinary values of type `Result`, returned by the function that failed. The caller handles the error or passes it on with the `?` operator, and the function's signature says which it might have to do. This chapter covers `Result`, `?`, error types of your own, and where warnings and `try()` fit. The matching chapter of the Rust book is "Error Handling" [@rustbook, chap. 9].

## Errors as values

Converting text to a number can fail. R returns `NA` with a warning:

```{r}
#| label: r-parse
as.numeric("2.5")
as.numeric("twelve")
```

Rust's `parse()` returns a `Result`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-parse
println!("{:?}", "2.5".parse::<f64>());
println!("{:?}", "twelve".parse::<f64>());

match "twelve".parse::<f64>() {
    Ok(x) => println!("got {x}"),
    Err(e) => println!("error: {e}"),
}
```

Rust's `Result<T, E>` is an enum with two variants: `Ok`, holding a value of type `T`, and `Err`, holding an error of type `E`. It's built the way `Option` is (@sec-missingness), with `Err` in place of `None` and an explanation inside. You've seen it before: @sec-types printed the results of `parse()`, and the constructors in @sec-s4 returned `Result<Normal, String>`. Handling one uses the same tools as `Option`: `match` (@sec-enums), `if let`, `unwrap_or()`, and `expect()`. Printed with `{}`, `parse()`'s error says "invalid float literal".

::: {.callout-note title="An R habit to drop in Rust"}
In R, `as.numeric("twelve")` doesn't stop. It produces an `NA`, and the warning is easy to miss, especially when it scrolls past in a long script or is converted inside a larger computation. Rust's `parse()` gives you no number at all until you've decided what happens when there isn't one.
:::

## Passing errors up with `?`

Most functions that call something fallible don't handle the error themselves; they pass it to their own caller. In R, that happens without any code. Here the error raised in `parse_number()` passes through `parse_normal()`, which has no code to forward it, and `try()` prints each error so that the later calls still run:

```{r}
#| label: r-propagate
parse_number <- function(text) {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(text))
  if (is.na(x)) stop("'", trimws(text), "' is not a number")
  x
}

parse_normal <- function(text) {
  parts <- strsplit(text, ",")[[1]]
  if (length(parts) != 2) stop("expected mean, sd")
  mean <- parse_number(parts[1])
  sd <- parse_number(parts[2])
  if (sd <= 0) stop("sd must be positive, not ", sd)
  list(mean = mean, sd = sd)
}

str(parse_normal("0, 1"))
try(parse_normal("0, one"))
try(parse_normal("0, -1"))
try(parse_normal("0"))
```

In Rust, `?` passes an error up:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-question-mark
use std::error::Error;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Normal {
    mean: f64,
    sd: f64,
}

impl Normal {
    fn new(mean: f64, sd: f64) -> Result<Normal, String> {
        if sd > 0.0 {
            Ok(Normal { mean, sd })
        } else {
            Err(format!("sd must be positive, not {sd}"))
        }
    }
}

fn parse_normal(text: &str) -> Result<Normal, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let parts: Vec<&str> = text.split(",").collect();
    if parts.len() != 2 {
        return Err(Box::from("expected mean, sd"));
    }
    let mean: f64 = parts[0].trim().parse()?;
    let sd: f64 = parts[1].trim().parse()?;
    let dist = Normal::new(mean, sd)?;
    Ok(dist)
}

fn main() {
    let inputs = vec!["0, 1", "0, one", "0, -1", "0"];
    for text in inputs {
        match parse_normal(text) {
            Ok(dist) => println!("{:?}", dist),
            Err(e) => println!("error: {e}"),
        }
    }
}
```

The `?` operator goes after an expression that produces a `Result`. If the result is `Ok`, `?` takes the value out, and the function carries on. If it's `Err`, the function returns that error immediately. The operator works only in a function whose return type can carry the failure: a `Result` for a `Result`, or an `Option` for an `Option`, where `None` returns early. Either way, the possibility of failure shows up in the signature of every function the error passes through.

The return type `Box<dyn Error>` is a trait object (@sec-generics): a boxed value of any type that implements the standard library's `Error` trait. Rust's `parse()` fails with a `ParseFloatError` and `Normal::new()` with a `String`, and `?` converts both into a `Box<dyn Error>` on the way out. The length check builds its error the same way, with `Box::from()`. That makes `Box<dyn Error>` a convenient return type when a function can fail in several ways and its callers only need the message.

The conversions come from the `From` trait, which the standard library implements for any error type and for text. Where no conversion exists, `?` doesn't compile, and `map_err()`, later in this chapter, converts the error by hand.

As when a panic unwinds (@sec-drop), the values a function owns are dropped when `?` returns early, so cleanup still happens. Because `?` is an ordinary return, this holds even in a program built to abort on a panic:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-question-mark-drop
# struct Connection {
#     name: String,
# }
#
# impl Drop for Connection {
#     fn drop(&mut self) {
#         println!("closing {}", self.name);
#     }
# }
#
fn read_sd(text: &str) -> Result<f64, std::num::ParseFloatError> {
    let conn = Connection { name: String::from("data.csv") };
    let sd: f64 = text.parse()?;
    println!("read {sd}");
    Ok(sd)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", read_sd("one"));
}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
In R, any function can raise an error, and the error passes through every caller that doesn't catch it, whether or not those callers were written with failure in mind. In Rust, a function that can fail says so in its return type, and each caller chooses visibly what to do: handle the error, or pass it on with `?`. Ignoring it by accident draws a compiler warning: calling a function that returns a `Result` and doing nothing with the result gives "unused `Result` that must be used". Ignoring it on purpose takes `let _ =` (@sec-drop).
:::

## `main()` can return a `Result`

The `main()` function itself can return a `Result`, which lets it use `?`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-main-result
#| error: true
use std::error::Error;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let sd: f64 = "one".parse()?;
    println!("{sd}");
    Ok(())
}
```

When `main()` returns an error, the program prints it, prefixed with `Error:` and in its `{:?}` form, and exits with a nonzero status, as an `Rscript` run that ends in an error does. The empty value, `()`, is written the same way as its type, so `Ok(())` means "succeeded, with nothing to return".

That also explains the `fmt::Result` returned by `fmt()` in @sec-display. It's a `Result<(), fmt::Error>`: writing the text either succeeds with nothing to return or fails with a `fmt::Error`. The `write!` macro returns one, which is why `fmt()` could end with a `write!` call and no semicolon.

## Error types of your own

R conditions have classes, and `tryCatch()` can handle one class of error and let the rest pass. R's `errorCondition()` creates an error with a class and extra fields:

```{r}
#| label: r-condition-class
check_sd <- function(sd) {
  if (sd <= 0) {
    stop(errorCondition(paste("sd must be positive, not", sd),
                        class = "invalid_sd", sd = sd))
  }
  sd
}

tryCatch(check_sd(-2), invalid_sd = function(e) {
  cat("sd", e$sd, "is invalid; using 1\n")
  1
})
```

In Rust, the kinds of error a function can return are the variants of an enum, and handling one kind is a `match` arm:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-error-enum
use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum DistError {
    NotANumber(String),
    InvalidSd(f64),
}

impl fmt::Display for DistError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            DistError::NotANumber(text) => {
                write!(f, "{text:?} is not a number")
            }
            DistError::InvalidSd(sd) => {
                write!(f, "sd must be positive, not {sd}")
            }
        }
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for DistError {}

fn parse_sd(text: &str) -> Result<f64, DistError> {
    let sd: f64 = text
        .trim()
        .parse()
        .map_err(|_| DistError::NotANumber(text.to_string()))?;
    if sd > 0.0 {
        Ok(sd)
    } else {
        Err(DistError::InvalidSd(sd))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let inputs = vec!["2", "two", "-2"];
    for text in inputs {
        match parse_sd(text) {
            Ok(sd) => println!("sd = {sd}"),
            Err(DistError::InvalidSd(sd)) => {
                println!("sd {sd} is invalid; using 1")
            }
            Err(e) => println!("error: {e}"),
        }
    }
}
```

The pieces:

- `DistError` lists the ways `parse_sd()` can fail, and each variant carries the details, as `sd = sd` added a field to the R condition.
- `impl fmt::Display` gives each error a message (@sec-display).
- `impl std::error::Error for DistError {}` makes it a standard error type, so it works with `Box<dyn Error>` and `?` in other functions. The braces are empty because every method of the `Error` trait has a default (@sec-s3-traits).
- `map_err()` converts one error into another, here the `ParseFloatError` into a `NotANumber` that records the text. Its closure ignores the original error with `_`. Then `?` returns the new error, if there's one.
- In `main()`, the second arm handles `InvalidSd` by falling back to 1, and the last arm handles everything else, like a `tryCatch()` with an `invalid_sd` handler and an `error` handler.

Because the error type lists every variant, the compiler checks that a `match` covers them all (@sec-enums). R's condition classes can't be checked that way: nothing records which classes a function might signal.

## `panic!` or `Result`?

The Rust book's guidance comes down to whether the failure is a bug [@rustbook, sec. 9.3]. Return a `Result` when failure is something a caller could reasonably handle: bad input, a missing file, a value out of range. Panic when continuing would mean working with a state the code was never meant to be in, which signals a mistake in the program rather than in its input. R has a looser version of the same line: `stopifnot()` for terse, assertion-style checks, and `stop()` for a message aimed at whoever has to fix the input. Both raise ordinary errors that `tryCatch()` can handle.

Rust's `unwrap()` and `expect()` turn a `Result` into a panic: they return the value inside an `Ok` and panic on an `Err`. They suit examples, quick scripts, and places where an error really would be a bug. Of the two, `expect()` is better, because its message says what was expected:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-expect
#| error: true
let sd: f64 = "two".parse().expect("the sd should be a number");
```

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
R's `try()` turns an error into a value. It returns the result if the expression succeeds and an object of class `"try-error"` if it fails:

```{r}
#| label: r-try
result <- try(log("a"), silent = TRUE)
class(result)
inherits(result, "try-error")
```

That's a `Result` in all but name. The difference is that nothing makes you check which one you got. Code that forgets `inherits(result, "try-error")` carries on with the error object as if it were the answer. A Rust value sits inside the `Ok`, so code can't use it without saying what happens on an `Err`.
:::

## Warnings

R's `warning()` has no direct counterpart in Rust. A warning lets a function continue while telling someone that something is off, and Rust has no built-in channel for that. A program can print a message to standard error with `eprintln!`, which works like `println!`. A library can return the information instead, for example in a field of the result, so that the caller decides whether to report it. Larger programs use a logging library.

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `stop()` | Return `Err(...)`, or `panic!` for bugs |
| `as.numeric("x")` gives `NA` and a warning | `parse()` returns a `Result` |
| Errors pass through callers on their own | `?` passes an error up, visibly |
| `tryCatch(expr, error = ...)` | `match` on `Ok` and `Err` |
| `on.exit()` runs on error | Values are dropped when `?` returns |
| Condition classes, `errorCondition()` | An error enum, matched by variant |
| A handler for one condition class | A `match` arm for one variant |
| `try()` returns a `"try-error"` object | `Result`, whose value can't be used until `Err` is handled |
| `stopifnot()` | `expect()`, or `assert!` (@sec-macros) |
| `warning()` | `eprintln!`, or information in the result |
| `Rscript` exits with an error status | `main()` returns `Err` |
